name: Tony Blair
role: UK prime minister (1997–2007) and Labour leader (1994–2007); executive chairman of the Tony Blair Institute for Global Change
summary: Tony Blair led Labour to three election wins on a 'New Labour' or Third Way programme that kept market economics and union reforms of the 1980s while raising spending on health and education, adding a minimum wage, devolution and the Human Rights Act. He favoured open, interdependent globalisation, liberal interventionism (Kosovo, Sierra Leone, Iraq), a close US alliance and a pro-European line. Since leaving office he has argued for technology-led state reform, a more cautious climate strategy and, after the Brexit vote, tighter immigration controls.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Labour manifestos he led (1997, 2001, 2005) pledge to protect and fund the NHS; in his 2002 conference speech he calls for 'an NHS true to the principle of care on the basis of need, not ability to pay'.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Embraced market competition and an 'open, liberal economy' (2005) and rewrote Clause IV to pair enterprise with justice, while also arguing for large state investment in public services; his view is a qualified, not absolute, preference for markets.

public-ownership.rationale: Personally drove the 1995 replacement of Clause IV, which had called for common ownership of industry; the 1997 manifesto kept the privatised utilities (with a windfall levy and regulation) and his 2002 speech says 'Out goes the Big State'.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Manifestos he led in 1997, 2001 and 2005 each pledged not to raise the basic or top rate of income tax.

cut-welfare.rationale: Mixed: his 2002 speech calls for ending a 'culture of benefits and entitlements' and welfare reform, but he also expanded tax credits, child benefit and pensioner support and rejected an 'ungenerous benefit system'.

legalize-drugs.rationale: In 2000 he said of decriminalising or legalising cannabis, 'I am against it', warning it 'would not stop at soft drugs'.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: 2005 manifesto commits to legislate to outlaw incitement to hatred on grounds of religion and cites racially aggravated offences; 1997 manifesto promised new offences of racial harassment and racially motivated violence.

limit-guns.rationale: 1997 manifesto: 'only the strictest firearms laws can provide maximum safety' and called for an outright ban on handguns; 2005 manifesto notes 'we have banned all handguns' and promises more.

empower-police-military.rationale: His governments raised police numbers to record levels and added new powers (anti-social behaviour orders, 2005 anti-extremism measures); 2005 manifesto promises more police and forces 'the most flexible and effective in the world'.

traditional-family.rationale: 1997 manifesto: 'Families are the core of our society' and 2001: 'marriage provides a strong foundation for stable relationships', but his governments also backed civil partnerships, so 'traditional' structures are not his sole emphasis.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: His government passed civil partnerships (2004); in 2014 he said it is 'right now to take [civil partnerships] to a further stage' and praised the government for doing so, and that equal treatment is 'something I believe in'.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Mixed over time: in office he said migration made Britain stronger while keeping controls, but in 2017-18 he proposed registration, job-offer requirements and an emergency brake to 'curtail' EU immigration; the later position is used.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: 1999 Chicago: wants the UN reformed and states to accept 'the judgements of international organisations even when you do not like them'; 2002 he says ignoring the UN would destroy its authority.

free-trade.rationale: 1999 Chicago speech calls for a new push on free trade and says protectionism leads to poverty; his 2002 speech wants a coalition for 'free trade, free markets and free enterprise'.

nation-first.rationale: 2002 speech: 'it is a delusion that national identity is best preserved in isolation' and interdependence forces us to 'locate that interest in the wider international community'.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: 1999 Chicago speech sets out when to 'get actively involved in other people's conflicts', defending the Kosovo war as 'a just war... based on values'; in 2007 he cites Kosovo and Sierra Leone as decisions to intervene.

open-borders.rationale: 2005 speech: 'we know we need strict controls', with ID cards; 2006: 'If you come here lawfully, we welcome you'; no stated aim of open borders.

limit-growth.rationale: His 2025 Tony Blair Institute report foreword calls any strategy based on limiting consumption or quickly phasing out fossil fuels 'doomed to fail'.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Mixed: 1997 and 2002 he pledged to lead on global warming and a 20 per cent CO2 cut, but his 2025 foreword calls the climate debate 'irrational' and rejects short-term phase-out of fossil fuels in favour of carbon capture and nuclear.

expand-nuclear.rationale: 1997 manifesto saw no case for new nuclear stations, but the 2005 manifesto counts nuclear in the energy mix and in 2025 he proposes nuclear power alongside carbon capture instead of stopping fossil-fuel production.

experts-over-public.rationale: On Times Radio in 2023 he backed a powerful science and innovation body of 'people who know what they're talking about' as in short supply in politics, in a report with William Hague.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: 2005 conference speech: the temptation 'to protect... an industry by tariffs... doesn't work'; 1999 Chicago: 'Protectionism is the swiftest road to poverty.'

separate-church-state.rationale: His governments expanded faith schools (2001 manifesto: more church schools; 2002 speech lists faith schools), and his 2006 speech has faith schools twin and teach religious education, so religion and state are not strictly separated.

results-over-ideology.rationale: 1997 manifesto: 'New Labour is a party of ideas and ideals but not of outdated ideology. What counts is what works.'

universal-morality.rationale: 2002: values of democracy, freedom, tolerance and justice 'aren't western values. They're human values', held across cultures.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: 1997 manifesto pledged that over the cycle government would only borrow to invest and keep public debt at a stable, prudent level, and criticised the doubling of national debt.

force-without-un.rationale: Took Britain to war in Iraq in 2003 without a new Security Council resolution authorising force, arguing existing resolutions sufficed and that a second one was not legally necessary; he did not claim he would act with no UN basis at all.

work-for-welfare.rationale: 1997 manifesto pledged a modern welfare state 'based on rights and duties going together' and a welfare-to-work programme; 2002 speech calls for a 'partnership of rights and responsibilities'.

class-collaboration.rationale: 1997 manifesto: 'our aim is partnership not conflict between employers and employees' and an aim to end bitter struggles such as 'bosses versus workers'.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: 2006 speech: 'Integration... is not about culture or lifestyle. It is about values'; people have 'a perfect right to their own identity and religion' and 'the right to be different', alongside a duty to integrate around shared values.

proportional-representation.rationale: Mixed: introduced proportional systems for the Scottish Parliament, Welsh Assembly, European Parliament and London Assembly, but 1997/2005 manifestos only offered a referendum for Westminster, which he did not hold.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: 2006 speech names 'equal treatment for all' and 'equality of respect and treatment for all citizens' as essential values; his governments passed anti-discrimination law.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: 2006 speech: 'Nobody can legitimately ask to stand outside the law of the nation... no question of the UK allowing the introduction of religious law'; consensual religious arbitration with recourse to UK courts is allowed.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: 1997 manifesto: 'The key elements of the trade union legislation of the 1980s will stay - on ballots, picketing and industrial action.'

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: 2006 speech: multicultural Britain was 'never supposed to be a celebration of division; but of diversity' and 'integrating people whilst preserving their distinctive cultures... is the norm'.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Argued Britain must lead in Europe 'vigorous, confident' and campaigned to stay in the EU, while asking whether it would be 'a union of nation states or a centralised superstate' and keeping a referendum on the 2005 treaty.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: 1997 manifesto: 'Strong defence through NATO'; 2002 speech defends the Atlantic alliance ('I believe in this alliance and I will fight long and hard to maintain it').

death-penalty.rationale: In 2006 he said Britain opposes the death penalty 'whether it's Saddam or anyone else'.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Pressed at Gleneagles in 2005 for 100 per cent forgiveness of poor-country debts to international financial institutions; 1999 Chicago called for a serious examination of third-world debt.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Led the 2005 Commission for Africa and G8 push for a substantial aid increase and 100 per cent debt relief for poor countries.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Hansard, 28 June 2006: 'I believe that an independent nuclear deterrent is an essential part' of Britain defending itself; 1997 and 2005 manifestos retain Trident/the independent deterrent.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Gave the Bank of England operational independence in 1997 (manifesto pledged to reform it so monetary policy was free from short-term political manipulation); in 2002 he calls it a bold choice.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: 2002 speech called for talks aiming at 'an Israeli state free from terror... and a viable Palestinian state based on the boundaries of 1967'.

common-currency.rationale: 2002: 'We should only join the Euro if the economic tests are met... But if the tests are passed, we go for it.'

ban-cartels.rationale: 1997 manifesto promised 'a reformed and tougher competition law' with 'gains for consumers'; the Competition Act 1998 followed.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Mixed: pledged and passed the end of the hereditary principle in the Lords (1997, 2005), but did not abolish hereditary titles or the monarchy.

parliament-supreme.rationale: 1997 manifesto: 'A sovereign Westminster Parliament will devolve power to Scotland and Wales'; Parliament passed the Lords reform and Human Rights Act he led.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: 2002: 'Our values aren't western values. They're human values, and anywhere, anytime people are given the chance, they embrace them'; rejects claims Iraqis or Afghans do not want freedom.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: 1997 manifesto criticised the Conservative plan to replace the state pension with a privatised scheme and promised that 'the basic state pension will be retained as the foundation of pension provision', with a public-private partnership on top.

non-intervention.rationale: 1999 Chicago speech: 'the principle of non-interference must be qualified in important respects. Acts of genocide can never be a purely internal matter.'

public-access-to-information.rationale: Contested: promised and passed the Freedom of Information Act (1996 speech, 1997 manifesto), but in A Journey (2010) he calls it a mistake that undermined 'sensible government'.

national-law-over-international.rationale: 1999 Chicago: a rules-based system 'means accepting the judgements of international organisations even when you do not like them'; his government incorporated the European Convention on Human Rights into UK law.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: 2002 speech: universal free provision stays but 'the means of delivery, partnership between public, private and voluntary sectors' change; foundation hospitals, academies and PFI defended; 2005 manifesto promises independent specialist schools.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: 1997 manifesto aims 'to put behind us the bitter political struggles of left and right' and says its approach 'differs from the old left and the Conservative right'.

islam-incompatible.rationale: 2006 speech: 'Most Muslims are proud to be British and Muslim and are thoroughly decent law-abiding citizens'; extremism is an ideology of a minority.

social-market-economy.rationale: Rewrote Clause IV in 1995 to combine enterprise with justice and, in 1997, to 'put a commitment to enterprise alongside the commitment to justice'; his governments combined a market economy with a minimum wage, tax credits and competition law.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Committed in manifestos to strong forces 'through NATO' (1997) and to 'the most flexible and effective' armed forces (2005).

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Kept Britain in NATO and argued for the transatlantic alliance (1997 manifesto, 2002 speech).

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Led the Belfast (Good Friday) Agreement process; the 2005 manifesto calls it 'a remarkable achievement' and works to restore power-sharing between unionists and nationalists.

second-chamber.rationale: 1997 and 2005 manifestos: reform the Lords but keep 'a modern and effective revising Chamber'.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: 1997 manifesto: 'devolution not federation... A sovereign Westminster Parliament will devolve power', so devolved powers remain Westminster's to give.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Ordered force in Kosovo, Sierra Leone, Afghanistan and Iraq, defending the Iraq war as a pre-emptive response to WMD and terrorism rather than a response to attack.

free-public-college.rationale: His government introduced tuition fees and, in 2004, variable top-up fees, which Blair pressed through the Commons; in 2005 he said reforming university funding 'was tough' but 'the right thing to do'.

arms-reduction.rationale: 1997 manifesto: retain Trident while pressing for 'multilateral negotiations towards mutual, balanced and verifiable reductions in nuclear weapons'; 2005 manifesto pursues non-proliferation.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: His government introduced Working Families Tax Credit and its successors; the 2005 manifesto states 'tax credits and the minimum wage are ensuring that work pays' and his 2002 speech lists the credit among his anti-poverty measures.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: 1997 manifesto pledged to borrow only to invest, not to fund current spending, and the 2001 manifesto credits 'long-term fiscal rules' for stability; these were government rules he endorsed.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Renewed Britain's deterrent while saying 'there is nothing inconsistent in renewing our independent nuclear deterrent and in being in favour of non-proliferation'.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: 2006 speech: English should be a condition of citizenship and an English test required before permanent residency.

international-criminal-courts.rationale: 1999 Chicago: Britain will assist the war crimes tribunal 'to bring to justice those who have committed these appalling crimes' in the Balkans.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: 1997 manifesto: the future of Northern Ireland 'must be determined by the consent of the people'; the status question was settled by referendum in 1998.

notes: Living (born 6 May 1953, Wikipedia says age 73). Views that changed: immigration (no transitional limits on eastern Europeans in 2004; proposed curbs on EU immigration in 2017-18, most recent used), Freedom of Information (supported in 1996-97, regretted in 2010), nuclear power (no case for new stations in 1997; in the energy mix 2005; backed again in 2025). Iraq war and civil-liberties measures are contested; answers are limited to what he stated or enacted. A Journey (2010) and On Leadership (2024) were not available as full text; A Journey is cited only through a secondary article. Tony Blair Institute digital ID and AI proposals were not answered because no statement matches specifically.
